title: Treat a decisively-relied-upon score as triggering GDPR Article 22, and require evidence of genuine human deviation
description: Illustrative reference decision modelled on the CJEU's SCHUFA ruling (Case C-634/21). Not a documented decision of any specific organisation. Confidence rationale: 'Community' because this is an illustrative response, not a real organisation's adopted policy — the underlying legal holding it responds to is itself 'Reviewed' (see INC-021), a distinction this dataset keeps deliberately explicit.
decision_statement: Any score or recommendation produced by an automated system, if a downstream decision-maker relies on it decisively (rather than meaningfully weighing it alongside independent judgement), must be treated as triggering GDPR Article 22's automated-decision-making safeguards — regardless of whether the scoring system itself makes the final decision.
decision_context: Motivated by the CJEU's SCHUFA ruling, which held that a credit bureau's score can itself constitute prohibited automated decision-making under GDPR Article 22 when a lender relies on it decisively, closing a gap where scoring intermediaries had argued they bore no Article 22 responsibility.
governing_body: Illustrative example — Automated Decision Accountability Board
alternatives_considered: Treat only the final decision-maker as subject to Article 22, leaving scoring intermediaries unregulated.
Accept a documented human-review step at face value without measuring whether reviewers ever actually deviate from the score.

citations.title: Judgment of the Court (First Chamber), 7 December 2023 — OQ v Land Hessen (SCHUFA Holding, Scoring), Case C-634/21
citations.publisher: Court of Justice of the European Union

relationships.reason: This decision is modelled directly on the CJEU's holding in this case.
The decision is put into practice via this single, primary design pattern — no secondary pattern is needed for this concept.
This decision is a direct application of the existing GDPR Article 22 control — a new control would inflate the mapping without adding meaning.
Compliance must be demonstrated by an observable human deviation rate, not asserted.
Boards adopting this decision should be asking whether human review is genuine or symbolic.
